name: Sleet-Pinnacle
description: Sleet-Pinnacle is a cold, rocky world where jagged mountain peaks rise like broken teeth from a barren landscape perpetually glazed with ice. The thin atmosphere allows only intermittent precipitation, but when it comes, it falls as sharp sleet that hammers the exposed rock with enough force to erode it into the planet's characteristic needle-like formations. Frozen methane lakes fill the low basins between mountain ranges, their surfaces cracked and refrozen in fractal patterns.

The thin air carries sound poorly, giving the world a muted, tomb-like quality. The sleet, when it falls, creates a brittle percussion against stone that is the loudest natural sound on the planet. Crystal caverns beneath the mountain ranges glow with internal phosphorescence, their walls lined with dark crystal formations that absorb light at certain wavelengths and re-emit it in patterns that seem almost deliberate.

A distress beacon has been broadcasting from a deep valley on the southern continent for at least fifteen years. Multiple rescue missions have located the signal source but found no wreckage, no survivors, and no equipment, only the beacon itself, mounted on bare rock with no visible power supply. Each mission has reported the beacon as deactivated upon departure, yet the signal invariably resumes within days of the team leaving the system.

The dark crystal deposits in Sleet-Pinnacle's caverns have unique optical properties that make them valuable for sensor technology. The persistent distress beacon has become a cautionary tale and a point of morbid curiosity, drawing investigators who inevitably leave with more questions than answers. The microbial life in the methane lakes suggests subsurface warmth that the geological surveys have not fully mapped, hinting at a more complex world than its bleak exterior suggests.
